text:
The ladies de Nevers and de Martigues, on leaving her house, went to the Queen-Dauphiness’s apartments; Monsieur de Clèves was there. That princess asked them where they had come from; they told her that they had come from Monsieur de Clèves’s house, where they had spent part of the afternoon with a great many people, and that they had left no one there but Monsieur de Nemours. These words, which they thought so inconsequential, were not so to Monsieur de Clèves. Although he must well have imagined that Monsieur de Nemours might often find opportunities to speak to his wife, nevertheless the thought that he was at her house, that he was there alone, and that he might speak to her of his love, seemed to him at that moment so novel and so unbearable that jealousy flared up in his heart more violently than it ever had before. It was impossible for him to remain with the Queen; he returned home, not even knowing why he was returning, or whether he intended to go and interrupt Monsieur de Nemours. As soon as he approached his house, he looked to see whether he might notice anything that would enable him to judge whether that prince was still there: he felt relieved when he saw that he was no longer there, and found comfort in thinking that he could not have remained long. He imagined that perhaps Monsieur de Nemours was not the man of whom he ought to be jealous; and although he did not doubt it at all, he sought to doubt it; but so many things would have convinced him of it that he did not remain long in the uncertainty he desired. He went at once to his wife’s chamber, and after speaking to her for some time about indifferent matters, he could not keep himself from asking her what she had done and whom she had seen; she gave him an account of it. When he saw that she did not name Monsieur de Nemours, he asked her, trembling, whether that was everyone she had seen, in order to give her an opportunity to name that prince and to spare himself the pain of her practicing a deception upon him concerning it. As she had not seen him, she did not name him; and Monsieur de Clèves, resuming in a tone that showed his distress, said to her:

“And Monsieur de Nemours—did you not see him, or have you forgotten him?”

“I did not see him, in fact,” she replied. “I was unwell, and I sent one of my women to make my apologies to him.”

“Then you were unwell only for him,” Monsieur de Clèves rejoined. “Since you saw everyone else, why make distinctions for Monsieur de Nemours? Why is he not like any other man to you? Why must you fear the sight of him? Why do you let him see that you fear it? Why do you make him aware that you are using the power his love gives you over him? Would you dare refuse to see him if you did not know very well that he distinguishes your severity from discourtesy? But why must you be severe with him? From a person such as you, Madam, everything is a favor except indifference.”

“I did not think,” Madame de Clèves replied, “whatever suspicions you may have concerning Monsieur de Nemours, that you could reproach me for not having seen him.”

“Yet I do reproach you for it, Madam,” he replied, “and my reproaches are well founded. Why not see him if he has said nothing to you? But, Madam, he has spoken to you; if his silence alone had revealed his love to you, it would not have made so great an impression upon you. You could not tell me the whole truth; you concealed the greater part of it from me; you even repented of the little you confessed to me, and you did not have the strength to continue. I am more unhappy than I believed, and I am the unhappiest of all men. You are my wife; I love you as my beloved, and I see you love another. That other man is the most lovable at court, and he sees you every day; he knows that you love him. Ah! I could believe,” he exclaimed, “that you would overcome the love you have for him. I must have lost my reason to have believed it possible.”

“I do not know,” Madame de Clèves replied sadly, “whether you were wrong to judge favorably of conduct as extraordinary as mine; but I do not know whether I was not mistaken in believing that you would do me justice.”

“Do not doubt it, Madam,” Monsieur de Clèves replied, “you were mistaken; you expected things from me as impossible as those I expected from you. How could you hope that I would preserve my reason? Had you then forgotten that I loved you desperately and that I was your husband? Either one of those two things can drive a man to extremes: what can they not do together? Ah, and what are they not doing!” he continued. “I have nothing but violent and uncertain feelings over which I have no control. I no longer find myself worthy of you; you no longer seem worthy of me. I adore you; I hate you. I offend you; I ask your forgiveness. I admire you; I am ashamed to admire you. In short, there is no longer either calm or reason in me. I do not know how I have been able to live since you spoke to me at Coulommiers, and since the day you learned from Madame the Dauphiness that your affair was known. I cannot make out how it came to be known, nor what passed between Monsieur de Nemours and you on that subject: you will never explain it to me, and I do not ask you to explain it. I ask you only to remember that you have made me the unhappiest man in the world.”

Monsieur de Clèves left his wife after these words and departed the next day without seeing her; but he wrote her a letter full of distress, honor, and tenderness. She made so touching a reply, so filled with assurances concerning her past conduct and the conduct she would maintain in the future, that, since her assurances were founded on truth and these were indeed her feelings, the letter made an impression upon Monsieur de Clèves and gave him some peace; moreover, as Monsieur de Nemours was going to join the King just as he was, he had the comfort of knowing that Monsieur de Nemours would not be in the same place as Madame de Clèves. Whenever that princess spoke to her husband, the love he showed her, the honorableness of his conduct, the affection she had for him, and what she owed him made impressions upon her heart that weakened the thought of Monsieur de Nemours; but it was only for a time, and that thought soon returned, more vivid and more present than before.

During the first days after that prince’s departure, she scarcely felt his absence; afterward it seemed cruel to her. Since she had loved him, not a day had passed when she had not feared or hoped to encounter him, and she found it very painful to think that it was no longer within the power of chance to cause her to meet him.
